title: Polymyositis: Diagnosis and Management
subject: Medicine
summary: Polymyositis is a chronic inflammatory myopathy characterized by progressive proximal muscle weakness. It is an autoimmune condition affecting skeletal muscles, leading to inflammation and necrosis of muscle fibers. Diagnosis involves clinical presentation, elevated muscle enzymes, and muscle biopsy.

sections.p: Polymyositis (PM) is a rare, idiopathic inflammatory myopathy primarily affecting skeletal muscles. It leads to progressive, symmetrical proximal muscle weakness due to inflammation and necrosis of muscle fibers. Diagnosis is based on a combination of clinical features, elevated muscle enzymes, characteristic electromyography (EMG) findings, and muscle biopsy.
b: Progressive, symmetrical proximal muscle weakness is the hallmark.
Muscle pain (myalgia) can be present but is not always prominent.
Dysphagia (difficulty swallowing) may occur due to pharyngeal muscle involvement.
Diagnosis requires exclusion of other causes of myopathy.

sections.p: Severity is assessed by the degree of muscle weakness, functional impairment, and systemic involvement. There is no universally accepted formal staging system for polymyositis, but clinicians categorize severity based on functional limitations and response to treatment.
b: Mild: Minimal functional limitation, good response to initial therapy.
Moderate: Significant functional impairment, requiring assistive devices or affecting daily activities.
Severe: Profound weakness, dysphagia, respiratory muscle involvement, or cardiac complications.
Disease activity is monitored by muscle strength, CK levels, and patient-reported outcomes.

sections.p: The exact etiology of polymyositis is unknown, but it is considered an autoimmune disorder. Genetic predisposition and environmental triggers are thought to play a role. It is not directly caused by infections common in low-resource settings, but these can complicate management or mimic its presentation.
b: Autoimmune process: Immune cells attack muscle fibers.
Genetic factors: Certain HLA types are associated with increased risk.
Environmental triggers: Possible role of viral infections or certain medications, though not definitively proven.
No direct link to HIV, TB, malaria, or schistosomiasis as a cause, but these must be considered in differential diagnosis.

sections.p: Patients typically present with insidious onset of muscle weakness, often over weeks to months. The weakness is symmetrical and predominantly affects proximal muscles, making activities like climbing stairs, lifting objects, or rising from a chair difficult. Unlike dermatomyositis, skin manifestations are absent.
b: Proximal muscle weakness: Difficulty with overhead activities, standing from a squat.
Fatigue and malaise are common systemic symptoms.
Muscle tenderness or pain may be present in some cases.
Dysphagia affecting the upper esophagus can lead to aspiration risk.
Respiratory muscle weakness can cause dyspnea and hypoventilation.
Cardiac involvement (myocarditis, conduction defects) is a serious but less common complication.

sections.p: Investigations aim to confirm muscle inflammation, exclude other causes of weakness, and assess for systemic involvement. In low-resource settings, prioritize readily available tests before considering more specialized ones.

t.b: Answers: Is there muscle damage? What is the extent? — Markedly elevated (often 10-50 times normal) indicates muscle breakdown. If unavailable, clinical assessment of weakness is paramount.
Answers: Is there systemic inflammation? — Often elevated, but can be normal in some cases. Useful for monitoring disease activity.
Answers: Are there other systemic issues or complications? — May show mild anemia of chronic disease or leukocytosis if infection is present. Eosinophilia can suggest parasitic infection.
Answers: Are there other organ involvements or drug toxicities? — Baseline assessment before starting medications. Can rule out hepatic or renal causes of weakness.

Answers: Is this an autoimmune myopathy? What is the specific subtype? — Anti-Jo-1 is common in polymyositis with interstitial lung disease. Anti-SRP is associated with severe, necrotizing myopathy. Often unavailable in low-resource settings; clinical and biopsy findings become more critical.

Answers: Is the weakness due to muscle disease or nerve disease? — Shows myopathic changes: short-duration, low-amplitude polyphasic motor unit potentials, spontaneous fibrillations, and positive sharp waves. If unavailable, clinical assessment and CK levels are key.

Answers: Confirms muscle inflammation and necrosis. — Shows endomysial inflammatory infiltrates (predominantly CD8+ T cells) surrounding and invading non-necrotic muscle fibers. This is the most definitive test but may not be available; if so, a strong clinical suspicion with elevated CK and typical EMG is often suffic
Answers: Is HIV-associated myopathy a possibility? — HIV can cause a similar myopathy. Essential in regions with high HIV prevalence. If positive, management differs.

sections.p: Early recognition of severe complications is crucial for preventing morbidity and mortality. These include respiratory failure, severe dysphagia, and cardiac involvement.
b: Progressive dyspnea or orthopnea: Suggests respiratory muscle weakness or interstitial lung disease.
Severe dysphagia: Risk of aspiration pneumonia and malnutrition.
New onset palpitations, chest pain, or syncope: Indicates potential cardiac involvement (myocarditis, conduction abnormalities).
Rapidly worsening weakness: May indicate severe disease or an acute exacerbation.
Signs of infection: Immunosuppression increases susceptibility to opportunistic infections.

sections.p: Management aims to suppress the immune response, reduce muscle inflammation, improve muscle strength, and prevent complications. Treatment is typically long-term and requires careful monitoring.
b: First-line: High-dose corticosteroids (e.g., oral prednisone) to induce remission. Taper slowly once improvement is seen.
Immunosuppressants (e.g., azathioprine, methotrexate, mycophenolate mofetil): Used as steroid-sparing agents or for refractory cases. Azathioprine is often more accessible in low-resource settings.
Physical therapy: Essential for maintaining muscle strength, preventing atrophy, and improving function once inflammation is controlled.
Nutritional support: For patients with dysphagia to prevent malnutrition and aspiration.
Treatment of complications: Manage aspiration pneumonia, cardiac arrhythmias, or interstitial lung disease as they arise.
Avoidance of certain drugs: Statins can exacerbate myopathy; careful consideration if co-prescribed.

sections.p: Regular follow-up is essential to monitor disease activity, assess treatment response, and detect complications or side effects of medications. Prevention focuses on early diagnosis and consistent adherence to treatment.
b: Monitor muscle strength and functional status regularly.
Track serum CK levels to assess disease activity and treatment response.
Screen for corticosteroid side effects (e.g., osteoporosis, hyperglycemia, hypertension).
Educate patients on medication adherence and warning signs of complications.
Encourage regular, gentle exercise as tolerated to prevent deconditioning.

sections.p: Polymyositis can be confused with other conditions causing muscle weakness or elevated CK. Careful differentiation is crucial for appropriate management.
b: Dermatomyositis: Similar muscle weakness but with characteristic skin rashes (e.g., Gottron's papules, heliotrope rash).
Inclusion body myositis: Typically affects older individuals, often asymmetrical weakness, distal muscle involvement, and poor response to immunosuppression.
Drug-induced myopathy (e.g., statins, alcohol): History of drug use is key.
Endocrine myopathies (e.g., hypothyroidism): Check thyroid function tests.
HIV-associated myopathy: Consider in endemic areas; often less inflammatory on biopsy.
Muscular dystrophies: Genetic conditions, usually with earlier onset and family history.
Neuropathies (e.g., Guillain-Barré syndrome): Primarily nerve involvement, distinct EMG findings.

sections.p: Interpreting results requires clinical context, as some findings can be non-specific or influenced by other factors.
b: Normal CK levels: Can occur in chronic, inactive disease or in some rare forms of myopathy, but typically markedly elevated in active PM.
Elevated CK from other causes: Strenuous exercise, trauma, seizures, myocardial infarction, or certain medications can also raise CK.
Non-specific EMG findings: Early disease or mild cases may have less clear myopathic changes.
Biopsy limitations: Sampling error can occur if the biopsied muscle is not representative of the disease process.

whenToSeekHelp: Sudden worsening of muscle weakness, especially affecting breathing or swallowing
Difficulty breathing or shortness of breath
Severe difficulty swallowing, choking, or coughing after eating/drinking
New or worsening chest pain or palpitations
Signs of infection (fever, chills, new cough) while on immunosuppressants

faq.q: What is the main difference between polymyositis and dermatomyositis?
faq.a: The key difference is the presence of characteristic skin rashes in dermatomyositis (e.g., Gottron's papules, heliotrope rash) which are absent in polymyositis, although both share similar muscle weakness.

faq.q: Can polymyositis affect organs other than muscles?
faq.a: Yes, polymyositis can affect other organs, most notably the lungs (interstitial lung disease), heart (myocarditis, conduction defects), and joints (arthralgia), though muscle involvement is primary.

Polymyositis is a chronic condition, and while not typically curable, it is treatable. The goal of treatment is to achieve remission, control symptoms, improve muscle strength, and prevent complications, often requiring long-term medication.

exam: A 45-year-old woman presents with progressive difficulty climbing stairs and lifting her arms overhead for the past 3 months. On examination, you note symmetrical proximal muscle weakness. Her CK is 8000 U/L. What is your immediate diagnostic approach in a low-resource setting, and what are your top three differential diagnoses? — Prioritize readily available tests: repeat CK, FBC, ESR/CRP, HIV test. Differentials: Polymyositis, HIV-associated myopathy, drug-induced myopathy

You suspect polymyositis in a patient, but muscle biopsy is unavailable. What combination of clinical and laboratory findings would strongly support your diagnosis to initiate treatment? — Strong clinical suspicion with progressive, symmetrical proximal weakness, markedly elevated CK (e.g., >1000 U/L), and typical myopathic changes on EMG (if available). Exclusion of other common causes is also important.

A patient with newly diagnosed polymyositis is started on high-dose oral corticosteroids. What are the key monitoring parameters you would track in the first few weeks, and what are two crucial patient education points? — Monitor muscle strength, functional status, and CK levels. Education: adherence to medication, potential side effects of steroids (e.g., weight gain, mood changes), and warning signs for infection.

During follow-up, your polymyositis patient develops new onset dyspnea and a persistent cough. What are your immediate concerns and how would you investigate them in a resource-limited environment? — Concerns: respiratory muscle weakness, interstitial lung disease, or opportunistic infection. Investigations: clinical assessment of respiratory effort, oxygen saturation, chest X-ray (if available), and sputum microscopy for TB (common in East Africa).

Distinguish polymyositis from inclusion body myositis based on clinical presentation and typical patient demographics. — Polymyositis: symmetrical proximal weakness, typically affects younger to middle-aged adults, good response to immunosuppression. Inclusion body myositis: often asymmetrical, involves distal muscles (e.g., finger flexors, quadriceps), affects older individuals, and is generally refractory to immunosuppression.

A patient with polymyositis is on long-term corticosteroids. What are two significant long-term complications you must screen for, and how would you manage them? — Complications: Osteoporosis (screen with DEXA if available, otherwise consider calcium/vitamin D supplementation, bisphosphonates) and hyperglycemia/diabetes (monitor blood glucose, dietary advice, consider oral hypoglycemics/insulin).

Why is it important to test for HIV in a patient presenting with myositis in East Africa, even if polymyositis is suspected? — HIV can cause a myopathy that mimics polymyositis, and its presence significantly alters management and prognosis. Immunosuppressive treatment for polymyositis could be detrimental in an undiagnosed HIV patient.

What is the role of physical therapy in the management of polymyositis, and when should it be initiated? — Physical therapy is crucial for maintaining muscle strength, preventing atrophy, and improving functional capacity. It should be initiated once acute inflammation is controlled and muscle pain has subsided, focusing on gentle, progressive strengthening and range-of-motion exercises.
